trip_options.title: Budget Explorer - Lisbon, Portugal
trip_options.description: Save money without sacrificing the experience. Perfect for travelers who value authentic local experiences over luxury.

experiences.description: Explore Portugal's unique artistic heritage through centuries of hand-painted azulejo tiles at this world-class museum housed in a stunning 16th-century convent. day_by_day.morning: Arrival at Lisbon Airport at 13:00 — no morning activities scheduled. Clear customs, collect luggage, and take the Metro (Linha Vermelha/Red Line from Aeroporto station) to central Lisbon for around €1.50 using a Viva Viagem card. Check in to Lisbon City Stay and freshen up.
day_by_day.afternoon: After settling in, take a leisurely walk through the historic Baixa-Chiado neighborhood. Stroll down Rua Augusta, pass through the grand Praça do Comércio overlooking the Tagus River, and soak in the city's atmosphere. Explore the narrow streets of Alfama at your own pace — free and full of history.
day_by_day.evening: Head to the Miradouro das Portas do Sol or Miradouro de Santa Luzia for a stunning free sunset view over Alfama and the Tagus River. Afterward, find a local tasca (traditional tavern) in Alfama for a simple, affordable dinner.

meals.breakfast: Grab a coffee and pastel de nata (custard tart) at a local café near the airport or hotel for under €2 — a classic Portuguese welcome.
meals.lunch: Pick up a bifana (pork sandwich) or a prego (steak sandwich) from a local snack bar in Baixa for €3–5.
meals.dinner: Dine at a local tasca in Alfama — look for a prato do dia (dish of the day) which typically includes soup, main, bread, and a drink for €8–12. Try bacalhau à brás (shredded codfish with eggs and potatoes).

day_by_day.notes: Buy a 24-hour or rechargeable Viva Viagem Metro card at the airport for easy transport. Keep Day 1 light — jet lag and arrival logistics can be tiring. Alfama is hilly, so wear comfortable shoes.

day_by_day.morning: Visit the National Tile Museum (Museu Nacional do Azulejo) — one of Lisbon's most unique and budget-friendly cultural gems. Explore centuries of hand-painted azulejo tile art housed in a stunning 16th-century convent. Entry is approximately €5 (free on the first Sunday of the month). Open from 10:00. Take Bus 794 or Tram 28E from central Lisbon.
day_by_day.afternoon: Head to the Time Out Market Lisbon Food Tour experience in the Cais do Sodré area. Spend a few hours grazing through Lisbon's iconic covered food market, sampling dishes from the best local chefs. Budget around €15–20 for tastings — try small plates of fresh seafood, petiscos (Portuguese tapas), and artisan cheeses. Browse at your own pace and enjoy the vibrant atmosphere.
day_by_day.evening: Walk along the waterfront LX Factory area (open late on Saturdays with markets and street food) or explore the Bairro Alto neighborhood, famous for its lively yet affordable bar scene. Enjoy a glass of local vinho verde or ginjinha (cherry liqueur) at a street-side kiosk.

meals.breakfast: Start at a local padaria (bakery) near the hotel — coffee + toast with butter and jam for under €3.
meals.lunch: Graze at the Time Out Market — budget €12–18 for a satisfying mix of small plates and a drink.
meals.dinner: Visit a Bairro Alto tasca for grilled sardines or caldo verde (kale soup) with bread and local wine — expect to spend €10–14 per person.

day_by_day.notes: The Tile Museum is a must for history lovers and is very photogenic. Time Out Market is busier on weekends — arrive by 12:30 to beat the lunch rush. LX Factory's Saturday market runs until late evening and is free to browse.

day_by_day.morning: Take Bus 727 or Tram 15E (included with Viva Viagem card, ~€1.50) out to Belém for a full morning of history. Visit the UNESCO-listed Jerónimos Monastery, a breathtaking masterpiece of Manueline architecture. Entry is approximately €10 (free on Sunday mornings before 14:00 for EU residents — check current policy). Explore the ornate cloisters and the tombs of Vasco da Gama and Luís de Camões.
day_by_day.afternoon: Walk five minutes to the iconic Tower of Belém (Torre de Belém), another UNESCO-listed Manueline monument standing on the banks of the Tagus. Entry is approximately €6. Afterward, stroll along the Belém waterfront and visit the Monument to the Discoveries (Padrão dos Descobrimentos) — exterior viewing is free. Take time to explore the riverside gardens.
day_by_day.evening: Return to central Lisbon and explore the Mouraria neighborhood — Lisbon's oldest and most multicultural quarter, full of character and affordable eateries. If available, look for a free or low-cost fado vadio (amateur fado) performance at a local restaurant or cultural center.

meals.breakfast: Stop at the legendary Pastéis de Belém bakery (open since 1837) right next to Jerónimos Monastery — the original pastéis de Belém cost around €1.30 each. Have 2–3 with a coffee for a perfect budget breakfast under €6.
meals.lunch: Grab a sandwich or a prato do dia at one of the casual cafés along the Belém waterfront — budget €7–10.
meals.dinner: Eat in Mouraria — look for a tasca offering a full meal with soup, main course (try frango assado/roast chicken or grilled fish), and a glass of wine for €10–13.

day_by_day.notes: Belém is about 6–7 km from central Lisbon — the tram ride is scenic and part of the experience. Arrive at Jerónimos by 10:00 to avoid crowds. Pastéis de Belém is always busy but the queue moves quickly. Confirm Sunday free-entry hours for monuments before visiting.

day_by_day.morning: Explore the São Jorge Castle (Castelo de São Jorge) — the medieval Moorish fortress dominating Lisbon's skyline. Entry is approximately €15 (discounts available). Walk the ramparts for panoramic views over the city and the Tagus River. The surrounding Alfama neighborhood is Lisbon's oldest district — wander its winding alleyways and discover hidden miradouros (viewpoints).
day_by_day.afternoon: Descend from the castle and explore the Feira da Ladra flea market at Campo de Santa Clara (open Tuesday and Saturday — if this falls on a Tuesday, great; otherwise explore the Intendente neighborhood and its beautiful Largo do Intendente square, a revitalized historic plaza with free public art and local shops). Visit the free Igreja de São Vicente de Fora church exterior and viewpoint terrace (small entry fee for the terrace, ~€5).
day_by_day.evening: Head to the Príncipe Real neighborhood for a relaxed evening stroll through its elegant 19th-century streets and garden square. Browse the Saturday organic market (if applicable) or simply enjoy the café culture. This area has some of Lisbon's best wine bars with affordable by-the-glass options.

meals.breakfast: Coffee and a tosta mista (toasted ham and cheese sandwich) at a local café near the hotel — €3–4.
meals.lunch: Pick up a hearty soup and sandwich or a prato do dia at a worker's café near Alfama — budget €6–9.
meals.dinner: Try a cervejaria (beer hall/seafood restaurant) in Príncipe Real or Rato area — amêijoas à bulhão pato (clams in garlic and white wine) or grilled fish with salad and local beer for €12–16.

day_by_day.notes: The castle walk involves steep cobblestone paths — sturdy footwear is essential. Combine the castle visit with Alfama wandering for a full morning. Monday can be quieter at most sites, making it a good day for popular attractions. Many national museums are closed on Mondays — plan accordingly.

day_by_day.morning: Visit the Feira da Ladra flea market at Campo de Santa Clara — Lisbon's famous open-air market held every Tuesday and Saturday. Browse stalls selling vintage items, antiques, azulejo tiles, local crafts, and curiosities. It's free to browse and a wonderful slice of authentic Lisbon life. Pick up affordable souvenirs like handmade cork items or vintage postcards.
day_by_day.afternoon: Spend your final afternoon revisiting your favorite neighborhood or exploring the Chiado district — home to the historic Bertrand Bookshop (world's oldest operating bookshop, free to enter), charming squares like Largo do Chiado, and the iconic A Brasileira café (have a coffee here for the experience — around €1.50 at the bar). Walk down to Cais do Sodré and enjoy the waterfront one last time.
day_by_day.evening: Enjoy a farewell dinner in Baixa or Chiado — splurge slightly on your last night with a proper Portuguese meal. Try a restaurant offering bacalhau com natas (creamy codfish gratin) or arroz de marisco (seafood rice). End the night with a ginjinha at one of the tiny ginjinha bars in Rossio square — shots cost around €1.50.

meals.breakfast: Grab a coffee and pastry at the market area near Feira da Ladra — local vendors often sell fresh baked goods for €1–2.
meals.lunch: Eat a light lunch at a tasca near Chiado — soup, bread, and a small main for €7–10, or assemble a picnic from a local mini-mercado with cheese, bread, and fruit for under €6.
meals.dinner: Farewell dinner at a mid-range tasca in Baixa or Chiado — a full Portuguese meal with wine for €15–20 per person. Toast to a wonderful trip with a glass of Alentejo red wine.

day_by_day.notes: Check flight departure time for the following day if applicable and plan transport back to the airport accordingly (Metro Red Line is the most budget-friendly option at ~€1.50). Leave time for any last-minute souvenir shopping. Bertrand Bookshop is worth a visit even just to say you've been inside the world's oldest bookshop. Keep some cash on hand — many small tascas and market vendors are cash-only.

trip_options.title: Classic Lisbon, Portugal Experience
trip_options.description: The sweet spot between comfort and value. Enjoy quality accommodations, diverse experiences, and good food.

day_by_day.morning: Arrival at Lisbon Airport at 13:00 — no morning activities scheduled. Clear customs, collect luggage, and take the Aerobus or Metro (Red Line to Green Line) to central Lisbon. Check in to Lisbon City Stay and freshen up.
day_by_day.afternoon: After settling in, take a leisurely stroll through the Baixa-Chiado neighborhood to get your bearings. Walk up to Miradouro de Santa Catarina for panoramic views over the Tagus River. Stop at a local pastelaria for your first pastel de nata and a bica (espresso).
day_by_day.evening: Head to the Time Out Market Lisbon for a relaxed first dinner — graze through stalls offering petiscos, fresh seafood, and Portuguese wine. A perfect low-key introduction to Lisbon's food scene without committing to a sit-down restaurant after a travel day.

meals.breakfast: On the plane or grab a quick snack at the airport upon arrival
meals.lunch: Skip or grab a light bite at a café near the hotel after check-in — try a tosta mista (toasted ham and cheese) at a local pastelaria for around €3–5
meals.dinner: Time Out Market Lisbon (Mercado da Ribeira) — budget €15–25 per person grazing multiple stalls; try bifanas, grilled fish, and a glass of Vinho Verde

day_by_day.notes: Flight arrives at 13:00. Allow 60–90 minutes for immigration, baggage, and transfer to the hotel. Keep Day 1 light to recover from travel. Metro + 1 transfer is the most affordable airport transfer (~€1.65 with a Viva Viagem card, which you should purchase at the airport for use all week).

day_by_day.morning: Start the day with the Alfama District Walking Tour & Fado Show (morning portion). Join a guided walking tour through Lisbon's oldest and most atmospheric neighborhood — wind through cobblestone alleys, visit the Largo das Portas do Sol viewpoint, and learn about Moorish history and the origins of Fado music. Visit the exterior of São Jorge Castle.
day_by_day.afternoon: After the tour, visit the Feira da Ladra flea market (open Tuesdays and Saturdays — if this falls on a Sunday, explore the Alfama independently and visit Igreja de São Vicente de Fora for its stunning azulejo panels and rooftop views). Wander down to the waterfront at Santa Apolónia for a coffee break.
day_by_day.evening: Return to Alfama for the Fado Show component of the experience — enjoy an authentic live Fado performance at a traditional casa de fado with dinner included or paired. This is the emotional heart of Portuguese culture.

meals.breakfast: At the hotel or a nearby café — try a galão (milky espresso) with a croissant or pastel de nata for €3–5
meals.lunch: A Tasca do Chico or any local tasca in Alfama — order the prato do dia (dish of the day) which typically includes soup, main, and bread for €10–14
meals.dinner: Fado dinner show in Alfama — expect €35–50 per person including the performance, dinner, and a glass of wine at a mid-range casa de fado such as Tasca do Chico or Mesa de Frades

day_by_day.notes: Book the Fado show in advance — popular venues sell out, especially on weekends. Wear comfortable shoes; Alfama's cobblestones are steep and uneven. The neighborhood is best explored slowly — allow time to get pleasantly lost.

day_by_day.morning: Full day dedicated to Belém. Take Tram 15E or Bus 728 from Praça do Comércio westward along the river (about 20–30 minutes). Begin with the Jerónimos Monastery — a UNESCO World Heritage masterpiece of Manueline architecture, built to celebrate Vasco da Gama's voyage to India. Arrive early to beat crowds.
day_by_day.afternoon: Walk to the Tower of Belém (Torre de Belém) along the riverside promenade — another iconic Manueline landmark and UNESCO site. Also visit the Monument to the Discoveries (Padrão dos Descobrimentos) nearby. Explore the waterfront gardens and enjoy the river breeze.
day_by_day.evening: Return to central Lisbon and explore the Príncipe Real neighborhood — a charming upscale residential area with independent boutiques, antique shops, and excellent restaurants. Enjoy a relaxed dinner in this quieter, locals-favorite district.

meals.breakfast: Stop at the world-famous Pastéis de Belém bakery (open since 1837) immediately upon arriving in Belém — the original custard tarts dusted with cinnamon are unmissable; 2–3 tarts + coffee for ~€5
meals.lunch: Cervejaria Ramiro-style seafood or a casual riverside restaurant in Belém — try grilled sardines or bacalhau (salt cod) for €14–20
meals.dinner: Taberna da Rua das Flores or similar tasca in Príncipe Real — seasonal Portuguese small plates and natural wines; budget €25–35 per person

day_by_day.notes: Jerónimos Monastery entry is free on Sunday mornings until 14:00 — but since this is Monday, budget €10 for entry. Tower of Belém costs €6. Consider a combined ticket if available. Belém is about 6km west of the city center — the riverside walk or tram ride is scenic and enjoyable.

day_by_day.morning: Visit the National Tile Museum (Museu Nacional do Azulejo) — one of Lisbon's most unique and beautiful museums, housed in a 16th-century convent. Trace 500 years of Portuguese azulejo tile art, from Moorish geometric patterns to Baroque masterpieces. The highlight is a 23-meter panoramic tile panel of pre-earthquake Lisbon (circa 1738).
day_by_day.afternoon: Join the Mouraria & Intendente Neighborhood Food & History Walk. Discover Lisbon's multicultural Mouraria quarter — the birthplace of Fado, once the Moorish quarter of the city. Taste traditional petiscos, learn about the neighborhood's layered history, and visit the revitalized Intendente square with its mix of old and new Lisbon.
day_by_day.evening: Explore the Martim Moniz and Mouraria area in the evening — the neighborhood comes alive at dusk. Visit the rooftop bar at Hotel Mundial for sunset views over the city, then head to a local restaurant for dinner.

meals.breakfast: Café Nicola or Pastelaria Versailles near the hotel — classic Lisbon café experience with coffee and pastries for €4–6
meals.lunch: Included or guided during the Mouraria Food & History Walk — expect tastings of local specialties such as caldo verde soup, bifanas, ginjinha (cherry liqueur), and regional cheeses
meals.dinner: Zé da Mouraria or a traditional tasca in the Mouraria quarter — hearty Portuguese home cooking; try cozido à portuguesa or grilled fish; €18–28 per person

day_by_day.notes: The Tile Museum is slightly east of the center — take a taxi or Uber for ~€7, or Bus 794. Tuesday is a great day to also check out the Feira da Ladra flea market (open Tuesdays and Saturdays) near Santa Apolónia if time allows before the afternoon tour. Book the Mouraria food walk in advance.

day_by_day.morning: Revisit the Time Out Market Lisbon Food Tour for a structured culinary deep-dive if not fully explored on Day 1, or explore independently. Spend the morning at the market tasting Portuguese breakfast items, artisan products, and chatting with vendors. Alternatively, visit the Chiado district for a final morning of café culture, bookshops (Livraria Bertrand, the world's oldest operating bookshop), and the Museu do Chiado.
day_by_day.afternoon: Take a scenic ride on the iconic Tram 28E through Alfama and Graça for a nostalgic city overview (buy your ticket on board or use your Viva Viagem card). Disembark at Miradouro da Graça or Miradouro da Senhora do Monte for the best panoramic views in Lisbon. Final souvenir shopping in Chiado or Baixa.
day_by_day.evening: Farewell dinner in the Bairro Alto or Chiado neighborhood — Lisbon's most vibrant dining and nightlife district. Choose a mid-range restaurant for a proper sit-down Portuguese meal to cap the trip. After dinner, enjoy a final drink at a rooftop bar or a traditional ginjinha shot at A Ginjinha near Rossio square.

meals.breakfast: Time Out Market or Café A Brasileira in Chiado — a historic literary café; coffee and pastry for €4–6
meals.lunch: Light lunch at the Time Out Market or a petiscos bar in Chiado — mix of small plates; €12–18 per person
meals.dinner: Taberna da Rua das Flores, Zé da Mouraria, or Restaurante Cervejaria Trindade in Bairro Alto — a classic Lisbon farewell meal with bacalhau, grilled meat, and Portuguese wine; €28–40 per person

day_by_day.notes: Tram 28E is very popular with tourists — expect queues in peak season. For a more authentic experience, ride it early morning or take Bus 737 which follows a similar route with fewer crowds. If departing Lisbon on Day 6, confirm checkout time and store luggage at the hotel if needed for a half-day of final exploration.

highlights: Mix of paid and free experiences

day_by_day.morning: Arrival at Lisbon Airport at 13:00 — no morning activities scheduled. Private airport transfer arranged to Lisbon City Stay. Take time to check in, freshen up, and settle into your luxury accommodations.
day_by_day.afternoon: After settling in, take a leisurely stroll through the Chiado and Baixa districts near the hotel. Visit the iconic Praça do Comércio waterfront square and enjoy the Tagus River views. Stop into historic Livraria Bertrand, the world's oldest operating bookshop, for a cultural first impression of Lisbon.
day_by_day.evening: Alfama District Walking Tour & Fado Show — Join an intimate guided evening walk through Lisbon's oldest and most atmospheric neighborhood, winding through narrow cobblestone streets, past ancient Moorish walls and colorful tiled facades. End the night at a premium Fado house for a soul-stirring live performance paired with Portuguese wine.

meals.breakfast: Not applicable — in-flight or at airport upon arrival.
meals.lunch: Light welcome lunch at the hotel or a nearby café such as Café Lisboa at the São Carlos National Theatre — enjoy a classic bifana sandwich or soup to ease into local flavors.
meals.dinner: Dinner included as part of the Fado Show experience, or dine beforehand at Páteo, the refined restaurant inside Bairro Alto Hotel, featuring contemporary Portuguese cuisine with impeccable wine pairings.

day_by_day.notes: Request a private luxury transfer from the airport in advance. Confirm Fado show reservation ahead of time as premium tables book quickly. Dress smart-casual for the Fado house.

day_by_day.morning: Belém Historical Monuments & Pastéis de Belém — Take a private car or scenic tram ride to the Belém district. Begin with a guided visit to the UNESCO-listed Jerónimos Monastery, a breathtaking example of Manueline architecture commissioned by King Manuel I. Follow with a visit to the iconic Tower of Belém standing sentinel on the Tagus riverbank. Finish the morning with the non-negotiable pilgrimage to the original Pastéis de Belém bakery for warm, freshly baked custard tarts dusted with cinnamon.
day_by_day.afternoon: Return to central Lisbon and visit the National Tile Museum (Museu Nacional do Azulejo) — Immerse yourself in Portugal's extraordinary azulejo tile tradition spanning five centuries. Housed in a stunning former convent, the museum features a remarkable 23-meter panoramic tile panel depicting pre-earthquake Lisbon. A private guided tour is highly recommended for deeper historical context.
day_by_day.evening: Enjoy a relaxed evening in the upscale Príncipe Real neighborhood. Browse artisan boutiques and antique shops before settling in for a refined dinner.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at the hotel — opt for the full Portuguese spread with fresh pastries, local cheeses, presunto ham, and freshly squeezed orange juice.
meals.lunch: Lunch at Feitoria, a Michelin-starred restaurant in Belém with stunning riverside views, celebrating contemporary Portuguese cuisine and exceptional local ingredients.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Alma, Chef Henrique Sá Pessoa's Michelin-starred restaurant in Chiado — a masterful reinterpretation of Portuguese culinary heritage in an elegant setting.

day_by_day.notes: Book Feitoria and Alma well in advance. The Jerónimos Monastery can be crowded on weekends — arrive early. Consider hiring a private guide for both Belém and the Tile Museum for the most enriching experience.

day_by_day.morning: Mouraria & Intendente Neighborhood Food & History Walk — Discover Lisbon's multicultural soul on a guided walk through Mouraria, the ancient Moorish quarter and true birthplace of Fado. Explore hidden alleyways, ornate tiled buildings, and vibrant street art while learning about the layered history of this neighborhood from the Moorish occupation to the present day. Visit the beautifully restored Intendente square and its artisan shops.
day_by_day.afternoon: Time Out Market Lisbon Food Tour — Head to the legendary Time Out Market in Cais do Sodré for a curated grazing experience through Lisbon's finest food stalls. Sample dishes from award-winning chefs including grilled octopus, bacalhau croquettes, açorda, and artisan cheeses. Pair tastings with local wines and craft beers. This is the definitive modern Lisbon food experience.
day_by_day.evening: Sunset drinks at a rooftop bar such as TOPO Chiado or Sky Bar at Bairro Alto Hotel with sweeping views over the city's terracotta rooftops and the Tagus River. Follow with a late dinner at a premium restaurant.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at the hotel followed by a coffee stop at Versailles Café, a grand Belle Époque institution beloved by Lisboetas.
meals.lunch: Lunch is the Time Out Market Food Tour itself — a curated multi-course grazing experience across multiple stalls.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Belcanto, Chef José Avillez's two-Michelin-starred flagship restaurant in Chiado — one of Portugal's most celebrated fine dining experiences with a tasting menu that reimagines Portuguese culinary history.

day_by_day.notes: Belcanto reservations should be made weeks or months in advance. Wear comfortable walking shoes for the Mouraria tour as streets are steep and cobbled. Sunday markets in the area add a lively local atmosphere to the morning walk.

day_by_day.morning: Private guided visit to São Jorge Castle (Castelo de São Jorge) — Perched on Lisbon's highest hill, this Moorish-era castle offers panoramic views over the entire city and the Tagus estuary. Explore the medieval ramparts, towers, and archaeological site revealing layers of civilization from the Iron Age to the Moors and Portuguese royalty. Descend through the atmospheric Santa Cruz neighborhood within the castle walls.
day_by_day.afternoon: Explore the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga (National Museum of Ancient Art) — Portugal's most important art museum, housing a world-class collection including Nuno Gonçalves' Panels of São Vicente, Flemish masterpieces, Asian decorative arts from Portugal's Age of Discovery, and exquisite Portuguese gold and silverwork. A private curator-led tour brings the collection to life.
day_by_day.evening: Leisurely evening in the Lapa and Santos districts — some of Lisbon's most elegant and historic neighborhoods. Visit the opulent Estrela Basilica at golden hour before heading to dinner.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at the hotel, then stop at A Cevicheria's neighborhood café or Café Nicola in Rossio for a mid-morning bica (espresso) and pastel de nata.
meals.lunch: Lunch at Solar dos Presuntos, a beloved Lisbon institution since 1976 specializing in traditional northern Portuguese cuisine — try the caldo verde, roasted suckling pig, or bacalhau com broa.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Loco, Chef Alexandre Silva's Michelin-starred restaurant offering a bold and creative tasting menu rooted in Portuguese terroir, featuring hyper-seasonal and locally sourced ingredients.

day_by_day.notes: Book Loco's tasting menu in advance. The castle is best visited on a weekday to avoid weekend crowds. Consider a private driver for the day to move comfortably between the hilltop castle and the museum.

day_by_day.morning: Sintra Day Trip — Take a private chauffeured excursion to the enchanting UNESCO World Heritage town of Sintra, just 40 minutes from Lisbon. Visit the fairy-tale Palácio Nacional da Pena perched dramatically above the clouds, and stroll through the lush romantic gardens. Explore the medieval Moorish Castle ruins for sweeping views over the Atlantic coastline.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue in Sintra with a visit to the mysterious Quinta da Regaleira — a neo-Manueline palace and gardens filled with esoteric symbolism, secret tunnels, and an iconic initiatic well. Return to Lisbon in the late afternoon for a final walk along the Avenida da Liberdade, Lisbon's grand Champs-Élysées-style boulevard, for any last-minute luxury shopping.
day_by_day.evening: Farewell dinner at a premium Lisbon restaurant, followed by a final evening stroll along the waterfront promenade at Ribeira das Naus, watching the lights of the 25 de Abril Bridge reflect on the Tagus.

meals.breakfast: Early breakfast at the hotel before departure to Sintra.
meals.lunch: Lunch at Incomum by Luis Santos in Sintra — a refined restaurant in a historic palace setting offering creative Portuguese cuisine using Sintra's celebrated local ingredients including queijadas and travesseiros pastries for dessert.
meals.dinner: Farewell dinner at Tasca do Chico, an intimate and authentic Lisbon tasca beloved for its exceptional bacalhau, honest Portuguese cooking, and occasional impromptu Fado performances — a perfect emotional close to the journey.

day_by_day.notes: Arrange the private Sintra transfer the evening before. Sintra's palaces require timed entry tickets booked in advance, especially in May. Pack a light layer as Sintra's altitude makes it cooler and mistier than Lisbon. Confirm hotel checkout time and arrange a private transfer to the airport if departing the following day.
